SeisFront Ontology: Documentation

SeisFront (Ontology of Seismic Fragilities) models the FEMA P-58 fragility categories as OWL classes, so that an OWL reasoner (or the DLIS set-based procedure) can assign fragility categories to BIM objects automatically.

Source: Acosta Reveco, Kwon, Sasibut & Brown, "Automated Fragility Classification of BIM Objects through Ontological Inference in Support of Seismic Loss Assessment".

Purpose and scope

Item

Description

Purpose

Define every fragility category as an OWL equivalent class, so that satisfying the class definition is a sufficient condition for membership. Classification then becomes OWL inference (instance retrieval / realization).

Domains covered

(1) Building design/construction information, with scope set by the IFC schema. (2) Seismic performance assessment, with scope set by the concepts needed to define FEMA P-58 fragility categories.

Current coverage

Hierarchy from D (Services) down to D2021 (cold/hot potable water piping) and its subcategories, plus D2022 (hot water service, heating). Presented as a demonstration; the method is intended to extend to all 764 P-58 categories.

Intended users

Engineers/researchers extending the fragility hierarchy, and developers integrating classification into BIM-based loss assessment workflows.

Ontology language

OWL 2 DL (developed in Protégé 5.6.x; consistency checked with HermiT).

Canonical URI

https://w3id.org/utoronto/ontologies/SeisFront

Code repository

SeisBimClass: https://github.com/joacostar/OntologyConsoleTestV2

 

Competency questions

1.      Which fragility categories does a given building component, with certain attributes, belong to?

2.      Given a fragility category definition, which building components belong to it?

Ontology Composition

The following figure shows how each ontology is connected to form the SeisFront ontology system.

•       sfront: imports bc:, sd:, dicm: and om2:.

•       bc: reuses prod: and imports an om2: subset.

•       sd: imports bc:.

•       sfa: links bc:/sfront: on one side to ifc: + ifcLit: on the other.

Important: om2: and dicm: are imported as subsets. Importing them in full slowed reasoning significantly, and importing the whole OM2 produced a logical inconsistency.

 

Source structure: the FEMA P-58 fragility hierarchy

•       The P-58 database contains 764 fragility categories, each coded with a letter A to F followed by digits (e.g. D2021.011a).

•       The hierarchy follows UNIFORMAT II, extended with attributes affecting seismic performance.

•       Every one of the 764 categories is a leaf node at level 5. Branch nodes above them (e.g. D2021, D202, D20, D) have no fragility functions of their own.

•       Extended hierarchy: SeisFront also defines intermediate branch nodes between D2021 and a leaf, created by varying one defining attribute at a time (e.g. D2021.0, D2021.01, D2021.011).

•       Partial classification: if the BIM data is incomplete, a component may only reach a branch node. That is still useful, since it narrows the candidate categories to the children of that node for the engineer to pick from.

Attributes defining D2021 categories

Attributes are not stored as fields in P-58; they are only found in each category's text description (e.g. "Cold or Hot Potable - Small Diameter Threaded Steel - (2.5 inches in diameter or less), SDC A or B, PIPING FRAGILITY").

Why connection type is omitted: it cannot be separated cleanly from diameter using the text alone, and BIM models much more often carry pipe diameter than joint type.

Why support type needs care: P-58 is inconsistent here. D2021.011b and D2021.012b are pipe plus bracing, while D2021.013b and D2021.014b are bracing only. This could not be derived from the text; it was inferred by inspecting the magnitude of the associated consequence (repair cost) functions.

Modelling pattern

Every category class follows one recursive rule:

Each fragility class is defined as owl:equivalentClass to (the class one level above) AND one or more property restrictions.

Consequences:

•       Subclass relationships (D2021.0 ⊑ D2021 ⊑ D202 ⊑ D20 ⊑ D) are not asserted. A DL reasoner infers them (shown as inferred arrows in Figure 9). The only asserted hierarchy is sfront:A to sfront:F under sfront:FragilityCategory.

•       Because definitions are sufficient conditions, any individual satisfying all restrictions is inferred to be a member.

•       The TBox is acyclic (each definition uses only earlier ones), which is what allows the fast DLIS procedure to be applied.

Properties and the component model

The Building Components (BC) ontology describes a component as follows:

Alignment to IFC (SeisFront Alignment, sfa:)

The alignment ontology contains only equivalence/sub-property axioms, so SeisFront itself never mentions IFC.

bc:MepComponent owl:equivalentClass [ a owl:Class ;

    owl:unionOf ( ifc:IfcBuildingElementProxy ifc:IfcDistributionElement

                  ifc:IfcMember ifc:IfcTransportElement ) ] .

 

ifc:IfcPipeFitting owl:equivalentClass prod:Fitting .

ifc:IfcPipeSegment owl:equivalentClass prod:Pipe .

 

bc:isInSystemOfType owl:equivalentProperty ifcLit:isInDistributionSystemPredefinedType .

ifcLit:hasPhysicalSimpleQuantity rdfs:subPropertyOf bc:hasAttribute .

ifcLit:hasProperty               rdfs:subPropertyOf bc:hasAttribute .

ifcLit:hasPropertySingleValue    rdfs:subPropertyOf bc:hasAttribute .

 

bc:ColdWater    owl:sameAs ifc:DOMESTICCOLDWATER .

bc:CoolingWater owl:sameAs ifc:CHILLEDWATER .

bc:HeatingWater owl:sameAs ifc:HEATING .

bc:HotWater     owl:sameAs ifc:DOMESTICHOTWATER .

 

Building data must be converted to ifcOWL + ifcLit (via the IFCOWLCONVERT tool) and supplemented with sd:hasSeismicDesignCategory triples before classification.

Worked example

An individual inst:IfcPipeSegment_10025 (an ifc:IfcPipeSegment, cold water, steel, SDC D) is classified into sfront:D as follows:

1.      sfront:D is equivalent to bc:MepComponent ⊓ sfront:VulnerableComponent.

2.      ifc:IfcPipeSegment ⊑ ifc:IfcDistributionElement, which is in the union defining bc:MepComponent. So the pipe is a bc:MepComponent.

3.      The pipe has sd:hasSeismicDesignCategory sd:SDCD, so it is a sfront:VulnerableComponent.

4.      Therefore it is inferred to be a member of sfront:D. Repeating the pattern down the hierarchy yields D20, D202, D2021, D2021.0, D2021.01, D2021.013 and finally the leaf D2021.013a.

To list the non-IFC classes an element belongs to, use a SPARQL query on rdf:type restricted to subclasses of sfront:FragilityCategory or bc:BuildingComponent (Listing 2 of the article).

The most specific class inferred is the classification of interest. It is written back to the IFC model as an IfcClassificationReference linked with IfcRelAssociatesClassification.

How to extend SeisFront

Suggestions based on Sections 3.3.1 to 3.3.4 in the article:

1.      Locate the category family in the P-58 fragility database spreadsheet (FEMAP-58_FragilityDatabase_v3.1.2.xls) and list all leaf descriptions.

2.      Extract defining attributes by comparing descriptions (system, material, size, SDC, supports, etc.). Where the text is ambiguous, check the consequence functions.

3.      Decide which attributes BIM models realistically carry. Drop those that rarely appear (as was done for connection type).

4.      Build the hierarchy by adding one attribute per level, ordering so each level's definition depends only on levels above it (keeps the TBox acyclic).

5.      Define each class as equivalentClass of (parent class) and (new restriction), using BC/SD vocabulary only.

6.      Add any new BC/SD concepts you need (e.g. new component classes or attribute classes).

7.      Extend the alignment ontology to map new BC terms to ifcOWL/ifcLit classes and properties. This step requires IFC knowledge.

8.      Add dc:description annotations with the P-58 text (used for readable reporting).

9.      Validate: check consistency with HermiT, then run competency questions and a test dataset.

10.   Re-run DLIS TBox reasoning (Step 1 of DLIS) whenever the ontology changes. It only needs to run once per ontology version.

Design rules to keep in mind

•       Use only the OWL constructs DLIS supports: intersection, union, oneOf, complement, and existential (someValuesFrom / hasValue) restrictions.

•       Keep definitions acyclic.

•       Avoid restrictions based on the absence of something (Open World Assumption). Assert absence explicitly instead (e.g. a wall class "without hold-downs").

Evaluation

Consistency: the full ontology system was verified consistent with the HermiT reasoner.

Competency questions, all passed:

Question

Expected

Which fragility categories apply to pipes (down to level 4)?

D2021, D2022, D2031, D2051, D2061

Which apply to pipes in domestic potable water service?

D2021, D2022

Which category applies to a pipe in no specific system?

Down to D20 (Plumbing) only

Which correspond to pipes with large diameter only?

D2021.02 and below; D2022.02 and below

 

Task-based evaluation: classification of the two-story clinic MEP model (Section 5) gave a micro-averaged hierarchical F1 of 98%. Remaining discrepancies came from IFC data quality (a distribution system exported with type HEATING instead of CHILLEDWATER) and from which of two diameter properties ("Diameter" 0.065 m vs "Outside Diameter" 0.0635 m) was read.

Limitations

•       Coverage: currently piping categories only (D2021, D2022). Conclusions should not be extrapolated to more complex categories (e.g. partition walls) without testing.

•       Manual expertise: writing definitions requires knowledge of the P-58 specifications and, for alignment, of IFC.

•       Not fully mechanizable: some distinctions (e.g. piping vs bracing-only) are only visible in consequence functions, which complicates NLP-based automation.

•       Open World Assumption: categories defined by the absence of a component need explicit assertions.

•       Data dependence: results are sensitive to IFC quality.

•       IFC version: implemented for IFC4; later versions can be supported via the alignment ontology.

•       Testing: validated on one realistic model.
